claims.subject: portrait_medium
claims.value: Bronze was a prestigious Roman medium for honorific portraiture and could support highly naturalistic characterization.
claims.confidence_reason: Supported by cited museum/heritage/specialist evidence at the stated scope.
claims.interpretation: Use bronze portrait behavior rather than applying marble bust treatment with a color swap.
prompt_implications: For a Roman bronze bust, preserve modeled portrait specificity, metallic depth, cast-and-finished surface behavior, and any inlay logic supported by the chosen example/context.

claims.subject: bronze_detail
claims.value: Roman bronze portraits could use contrasting inlays such as silver/copper for eyes or other details.
claims.confidence_reason: Supported by cited museum/heritage/specialist evidence at the stated scope.
claims.interpretation: Inlays are optional, context-sensitive details—not a mandatory decorative effect.
prompt_implications: If visible and appropriate, use restrained contrasting metal/stone inlays to support lifelike eyes or details; do not turn them into fantasy glow.

claims.subject: hairstyle
claims.value: Roman portrait hairstyles can be strongly date-sensitive and should not be treated as generic “Roman hair.”
claims.confidence_reason: Supported by cited museum/heritage/specialist evidence at the stated scope.
claims.interpretation: Strict reconstruction should narrow reign/century before asserting a specific coiffure as canonical.
prompt_implications: Use a date-sensitive Roman coiffure tied to the selected century/reign; if the date is broad, keep hair restrained and avoid overclaiming specificity.
